EC2-BOTL.c:
[Report] by the Hillside High School Student Council
In April, the student council installed three water refill stations in the school building, hoping to reduce the number of plastic bottles thrown away at school. Before the stations were installed, the school's recycling bins collected about 2,400 bottles every month.
As the table shows, the number of bottles collected fell sharply in the first few months. By July, it had dropped to 1,200, half the level before the stations were installed. Our goal is to cut the number by 60 percent by the end of the year, and we are confident that we can reach it if more students bring their own bottles.
We also counted how often the stations were used. In July, the counters on the three stations recorded a total of 9,000 refills.

[Comment] by Ms. Grant, school cafeteria manager
I am glad that fewer bottles are being thrown away. However, I would like to point out that the cafeteria also sold fewer bottled drinks in October, when many students were away on school trips. So part of the drop in October may not be due to the refill stations. Still, the stations are clearly popular, and I think the school should add one more station near the gym, where students line up for water after club practice.

EC2-LIBH.ti: 次の資料（“Longer Library Hours”：記事・表・コメント）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
EC2-LIBH.c:
[Report] by Daniel Ross, head of the Greenwood City Library
Since September, the Greenwood City Library has stayed open until 9 p.m. on weekdays instead of closing at 6 p.m. We made this change after many working adults and high school students told us that they could not visit during the day.
To see whether the change was worthwhile, we counted weekday visitors in each time slot in October, the second month of the new hours, and compared the numbers with October of last year. The evening hours are already attracting more than 2,000 visitors a month. We think the longer hours have been a clear success, and we plan to continue them next year.

[Comment] by Ms. Park, library staff member
The evening hours are clearly popular. But when I look at the numbers, I notice that fewer people are coming during the day than last year. The total has increased by only 1,500 visitors, even though we are now open 15 more hours each week. It is possible that some people who used to come in the afternoon now simply come in the evening instead. Keeping the library open longer also means higher costs for staff and electricity. I suggest that we ask visitors when they would most like the library to be open before deciding about next year.

EC2-MRKT.c:
[Report] by Lisa Chen, market organizer
The Riverside Farmers' Market opened in April last year in the parking lot next to the station. Every Saturday morning, about twenty local farmers sell vegetables, fruit, eggs, and bread directly to customers. In its first year, the market became a popular weekend spot for families.
The table shows the average number of visitors and the average total sales per Saturday in four months of last year. Visitors increased steadily from spring to autumn, and in October the market attracted 1,500 people a day. We plan to open the market on Sunday mornings as well from next spring. We believe that a second market day will bring even more people to the station area.

[Comment] by Tom Baker, owner of a grocery store on Station Street
I welcome anything that brings people to the station area, and the market has certainly done that. However, sales at my store on Saturday mornings have fallen by about 10 percent since the market opened, because some of my customers now buy their vegetables at the market. If the market opens on Sundays too, small shops like mine may suffer even more. I hope the organizers will consider ways for local shops to take part, such as giving us a few spaces in the market.

EC2-RAIL.ti: 次の資料（“The Future of the Ridge Line”：記事・表・コメント）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
EC2-RAIL.c:
[Letter] by Ken Mori, a resident of Maple Valley
The Ridge Line has connected our valley to the city for more than seventy years. Now the railway company says it may close the line because too few people use it. As the table shows, the average number of passengers per day has fallen from 1,200 in 2000 to 480 in 2020.
However, numbers alone do not tell the whole story. Many of the remaining passengers are high school students and elderly people who cannot drive. For them, the train is not a convenience but a necessity. If the line closes, some families may leave the valley, and the population will fall even faster.
I believe the town should help the railway company keep the line open, for example by paying part of its costs.

[Comment] by Ms. Hara, Maple Valley town planning office
I understand how much the Ridge Line means to residents. However, the line's annual loss has more than doubled since 2000, and the town's budget is limited. Instead of paying for a train that carries fewer people every year, the town could run a bus service that stops closer to homes, the hospital, and the high school. A bus would cost far less to operate. Of course, before making any decision, we must listen carefully to the students and older residents who depend on the line.

EC2-SLEEP.ti: 次の資料（“Screen Time and Sleep”：記事・表・コメント）を読んで、あとの問いに答えなさい。
EC2-SLEEP.c:
[Article] by Riko Sato, Northfield High School Newspaper
Last month, the health committee at Northfield High School asked all 400 students how they use their phones at night. The survey asked how many hours students spent looking at screens after 9 p.m., how long they usually slept, and whether they often felt sleepy in class. The results are shown in the table.
The pattern is easy to see. Students who spent less than one hour on screens after 9 p.m. slept an average of 7.2 hours, while those who spent three hours or more slept only 5.6 hours. In addition, 70 percent of the students in the heaviest group said they often felt sleepy in class.
The committee believes that the school should start a "Phones Off by 10" campaign. "If students put their phones away earlier, they will sleep longer and do better at school," said the committee leader.

[Comment] by Mr. Ellis, biology teacher
The survey results are worth taking seriously, but we should be careful about what they actually prove. The table shows that students who use screens late also sleep less. It does not show that screens are the cause. Some students may stay up late because they have club activities, part-time jobs, or a lot of homework, and they may simply use their phones while they are already awake. A campaign might help, but I think we should first find out why students go to bed late. In my opinion, a second survey that asks about homework and other activities would give us a clearer picture.

問題点を特定する：増加率は1,500÷11,000×100 で約14%であり、15%ではない。増加数の1,500から割合を直感で判断し、元の値で割っていない。
資料から言える範囲に書き直す：The number of visitors increased by about 14 percent (1,500 ÷ 11,000).

q.q:
次の英文が事実と意見のどちらを述べているかを判断する問題で、ある生徒は「事実」と答えた。
This is probably the most serious problem our town faces.
この判断の誤りを指摘し、正しい判断とその理由を答えなさい。
q.a: 意見である。probably（おそらく）と the most serious（最も深刻な）は推測と評価である。
q.e: 事実か意見かは、数値の有無や言い方の強さではなく、記録・調査・発言で確かめる方法があるかで決める。probably（おそらく）と the most serious（最も深刻な）は推測と評価である。
q.ea: 文を「確かめられる部分」と「書き手の評価・推測・提案の部分」に分け、文全体が何を伝えているかで判断する。
es: 文の中の数値・報告の語（said / predicted / complained）と、評価・推測・提案の語を区別する。
文全体が「確かめられる内容の報告」か「書き手の判断」かを決める。
正しい判断：意見である。probably（おそらく）と the most serious（最も深刻な）は推測と評価である。
